clinicalPearls: Suspect a work cause when asthma symptoms improve on days away from work, during holidays, and worsen on returning to the workplace

Two broad forms exist: sensitiser-induced disease, which follows a latency period of exposure, and irritant-induced disease that can follow a single high-level exposure (reactive airways dysfunction syndrome)
Common high-molecular-weight sensitisers include flour, animal proteins, latex and enzymes; frequent low-molecular-weight agents include isocyanates, colophony solder flux and certain wood dusts
Serial peak flow monitoring recorded several times a day at and away from work is a practical and valuable tool for confirming a work relationship
Early diagnosis matters because prolonged continued exposure after symptoms begin predicts persistent asthma even after removal
Complete removal from the causative agent, rather than simply reducing exposure, gives the best chance of recovery
A confident diagnosis has major implications for the worker's livelihood, so objective confirmation should be sought before advising job change
Consider workplace surveillance and review of coworkers, since others exposed to the same agent may also be affected
reference.pathophysiology: Sensitiser-induced occupational asthma develops through immunological sensitisation to an inhaled workplace agent, often IgE-mediated for high-molecular-weight proteins, leading to airway inflammation, bronchial hyper-responsiveness and reversible airflow obstruction on re-exposure. Irritant-induced asthma arises from direct toxic injury to the airway epithelium after intense exposure to a respiratory irritant, provoking inflammation and lasting hyper-responsiveness without a prior latency period.
additionalDifferentials: Non-occupational (constitutional) asthma coincidentally worsened by workplace conditions
Rhinitis with post-nasal symptoms mimicking lower airway disease
additionalInvestigations: Serial peak expiratory flow diaries covering periods at work and away from work
Non-specific bronchial challenge testing to document hyper-responsiveness
Specific IgE or skin prick testing to suspected occupational allergens where available
Specific inhalation (bronchial provocation) challenge in specialist centres when diagnosis is uncertain
Detailed occupational history including materials, processes and temporal pattern of symptoms
redFlags: Acute severe bronchospasm following a major irritant exposure or spill
Progressive symptoms despite continued exposure indicating risk of fixed airflow obstruction
Nocturnal attacks or falling peak flows suggesting poorly controlled disease
Features of anaphylaxis with certain protein allergens such as latex
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on how quickly the diagnosis is made and exposure stopped; early cessation gives a good chance of improvement, whereas prolonged exposure before removal is associated with persistent asthma and airway hyper-responsiveness that may not fully resolve.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to ordinary asthma and failing to take an occupational history
Advising reduced rather than complete removal from a sensitising agent
Relying on symptoms alone without objective serial lung function data
Delaying diagnosis so that airway changes become irreversible
Overlooking coexisting occupational rhinitis, which often precedes asthma
management: Complete removal from the causative sensitiser through relocation or substitution of the agent, which offers the best chance of recovery, as reducing exposure alone is insufficient
Standard stepwise asthma pharmacotherapy with inhaled corticosteroids and inhaled bronchodilators, adding systemic corticosteroids for exacerbations
For irritant-induced disease and unavoidable residual exposure, engineering controls and respiratory protective equipment
Serial peak expiratory flow and spirometry surveillance to confirm the work relationship and track lung function over time
Notification as a reportable occupational disease with advice on compensation, redeployment and workplace assessment
Referral to occupational and respiratory medicine, and screening of co-workers sharing the same exposure
